facts.text: On this date in 1947, the UN General Assembly voted to partition Palestine into Arab and Jewish states — a resolution passed with exactly the two-thirds majority required, 33 votes to 13.
On this date in 1986, the Iran-Contra affair became public when the White House admitted it had secretly sold arms to Iran and diverted profits to Nicaraguan rebels.
More people live inside a circle drawn around Dhaka with a 4,000km radius than outside it — that ring captures over half of all humanity.
Canada is the world's second-largest country by area yet ranks 38th by population, meaning its entire population could fit inside the city limits of Tokyo with room to spare.
The Philippines is the only country in the world where divorce remains entirely illegal for the majority of its citizens — Malta legalized it in 2011, leaving Manila uniquely isolated on the issue.
On this day in 1992, Lloyd's of London reported a £2.9 billion loss — then the largest in insurance history — triggering a crisis that nearly destroyed a market founded in a coffee house in 1688.
On Nov 25, 2008, the Fed announced its first quantitative easing program. Within six years, its balance sheet had grown from $900 billion to $4.5 trillion.
The NYSE was created in 1792 by 24 brokers signing the Buttonwood Agreement under a tree on Wall Street. The first stock traded was the Bank of New York.
Saudi Aramco's 2019 IPO raised $25.6 billion — a world record — yet it listed only 1.5% of the company, implying a valuation larger than the entire German stock market.
Berkshire Hathaway was originally a failing textile mill. Warren Buffett later called buying it the worst investment of his life, costing him an estimated $200 billion in opportunity cost.
On this day in 1915, Einstein submitted his field equations for general relativity — describing gravity not as a force, but as the curvature of spacetime itself.
On November 25, 1952, the first successful open-heart surgery using hypothermia was performed, cooling a patient's body to slow metabolism and buy surgeons precious minutes.
A neutron star packs more mass than the Sun into a sphere the size of a city — a single teaspoon of its material would weigh roughly a billion tons on Earth.
Your body replaces almost all its atoms every few years, yet the pattern persists. You are less a thing than a process, temporarily borrowing matter from the world.
Mantis shrimp see with 16 types of color receptors — humans have 3 — yet research suggests they process color worse than we do, using a entirely different visual logic.
On this day in 1952, Agatha Christie's 'The Mousetrap' opened in London. It ran continuously for 70 years — longer than the entire Victorian era it evokes.
On this day in 1963, JFK was buried at Arlington. The eternal flame lit that afternoon is still burning right now.
Oxford University was already 300 years old when the Aztec Empire was founded. Medieval Europe and 'ancient' civilizations overlap more than any textbook admits.
The fax machine was invented in 1843 — before the American Civil War, before the telephone, before Edison was born. We think of it as office furniture from 1991.
Cleopatra lived closer in time to the Moon landing than to the construction of the Great Pyramid. Ancient Egypt spans so long it swallows our entire concept of history.
Saudade (Portuguese): a melancholic longing for something beloved and lost. Untranslatable, it anchors an entire emotional culture — fado music exists largely to perform it aloud.
Hiraeth (Welsh): homesickness for a home you cannot return to, or never had. The word conflates grief, longing, and belonging into a single syllable cluster no English word touches.
On this day in 1952, Agatha Christie's The Mousetrap opened in London — giving English the word 'whodunit,' coined from the telegraphed question 'who done it?' in a 1930 US review.
Mamihlapinatapai (Yaghan): the shared glance between two people who both want something but neither will initiate. The language it comes from had, by 2022, one remaining native speaker.

Vellichor is not ancient — writer John Koenig coined it in 2013 for The Dictionary of Obscure Sorrows: the strange wistfulness of a used bookshop. Invented words can feel as inevitable as inherited ones.
On this date in 2017, Bitcoin's price crossed $8,000 for the first time — but more quietly, SegWit adoption on mainnet had just crossed 10%, the structural change that actually mattered.
On this date in 2021, the Ethereum network burned over 10,000 ETH in a single day for the first time since EIP-1559, making it briefly deflationary under high NFT demand.
Bitcoin's genesis block contains the text 'Chancellor on brink of second bailout for banks' — not as metadata, but embedded in the coinbase transaction, permanently on-chain since January 3, 2009.
The Lightning Network routes payments without recording them on-chain. A node can relay millions of dollars in transactions that leave zero trace on Bitcoin's base layer.
Ethereum's state trie — the data structure storing every account balance and contract — has exceeded 100GB. Syncing a full node requires processing this entire structure from genesis.

On this date in 2022, Stability AI released Stable Diffusion 2.0 — but the community largely rejected it, preferring the older 1.x models. User revolt over aesthetic quality shaped open-source AI development more than any corporate roadmap.
On this date in 1967, Frank Rosenblatt filed a patent for the 'Perceptron' — the direct conceptual ancestor of every neural network layer running inference today.
GPT-4's training run is estimated to have consumed more compute than all AI research published before 2012 combined. One model erased decades of collective effort as a rounding error.

Reinforcement learning from human feedback relies on a hidden workforce of thousands of contractors labeling outputs for toxicity and preference — their aesthetic judgments are literally baked into model weights.
The transformer architecture, now running nearly every frontier model, was introduced in a 2017 paper with eight authors. Six of the eight have since left Google.
